briefing.text: The token 'JP' in the hypothesis does not appear as an obvious value in the clinical tables of this MSK-IMPACT esophagogastric adenocarcinoma dataset. Before choosing a test group, search every column of the clinical, sample and mutation files (IDs, COHORT, CANCER_TYPE_DETAILED, ONCOTREE_CODE, SAMPLE_TYPE, site, abbreviations) for anything that could expand to JP, and list the COHORT categories. If JP maps to a subgroup, test that subgroup. If nothing maps, decide explicitly whether the hypothesis is about this study's disease, cohort and measurements under the benchmark convention (Not verifiable only when the claim concerns a disease, cohort or data type these tables do not cover), and state the mapping you chose in the reasoning.
briefing.reason: The scope decision comes before any analysis. If JP is silently mapped to an arbitrary subgroup, or the scope question is skipped, the label is wrong whatever the spectra show.

briefing.text: 'Dominant' must be defined before you look at the data, for example as the largest exposure share or more than 50% of SNVs in the pooled profile. SBS1 and SBS5 are present in almost every tumour, so finding them, or finding a positive age correlation, does not make them dominant. SBS5 is flat and soaks up unexplained mutations in NNLS fits. Compare the clock-like share (SBS1+SBS5) with the cancer-type hallmark (SBS17a/b) and with MSI and APOBEC signatures, and report the cosine similarity of the fit.
briefing.reason: The claim is about dominance, not presence. Without a definition set in advance and a comparison against the competing signatures, the conclusion is not grounded.

briefing.text: The aging (clock-like) signatures are SBS1 (C>T at CpG, from 5-methylcytosine deamination) and SBS5. In esophageal adenocarcinoma the hallmark signature is SBS17a/b (T>G, i.e. A>C, mostly in CTT context), and APOBEC (SBS2/13) and HRD (SBS3) also occur. A high overall C>T fraction does not by itself show aging. Compute the T>G fraction and split C>T into CpG and non-CpG contexts.
briefing.reason: This sets which spectral features separate aging from the other processes in this cancer type. Without it, a C>T-rich spectrum is easily misread as aging.

briefing.text: The mutations come from the MSK-IMPACT targeted panels (IMPACT341/410/468), and most samples have fewer than 10 SNVs. Per-sample de novo extraction or NNLS fitting is unreliable at these counts and overcalls flat signatures such as SBS5 and SBS40. Count SNVs per sample (Variant_Type==SNP) and report how many have at least 10 and at least 20. Pool SNVs across the cohort or subgroup into one profile before fitting, or restrict per-sample calls to samples with high counts.
briefing.reason: Fitting per sample on sparse panel data inflates SBS5 and so directly biases the aging-signature estimate.

briefing.text: Hypermutated outliers (MSI-high, POLE or very high TMB) can dominate a pooled spectrum. MSI signatures SBS6/15/26/44 are also C>T-rich. Inspect MSI_SCORE (10 or more is MSI-H in MSIsensor) and TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS in data_clinical_sample.txt, and report the share of all SNVs that comes from the top-TMB samples. Exclude MSI-H or hypermutated samples, or normalise each sample's spectrum before pooling.
briefing.reason: A few outliers can create or hide an apparent dominant signature in the pooled profile, so this changes how pooling must be done.

briefing.text: Targeted panels are enriched for selected driver hotspots, and many of them are CpG C>T (e.g. TP53 R175H/R248/R273, KRAS G12). These inflate CpG C>T and mimic SBS1. Recompute the spectrum after removing recurrent positions (same chromosome and start position in 2 or more samples), or keep only synonymous or passenger variants if any exist. If CpG C>T drops sharply, base the conclusion on the hotspot-excluded spectrum.
briefing.reason: Selection on driver hotspots can fake an SBS1-like signal, so this is a needed robustness check on any aging call.

briefing.text: A clock-like signature should rise with age. Correlate per-sample CpG C>T counts, or SNV counts normalised to panel size, with AGE_AT_SAMPLING, and adjust for panel version. IMPACT341/410/468 cover roughly 0.98/1.06/1.14 Mb (see data_gene_panel_matrix.txt), so do not compare raw counts across panels.
briefing.reason: Age correlation is the defining property of a clock-like signature and is a test that does not depend on spectrum shape. Panel normalisation is needed for it to be valid.

shared_assumptions: Both teams assumed that 'JP' has to appear as a literal token or a coded group in the tables before the hypothesis counts as being about this study. Neither tested what entity types 'JP' usually stands for in cancer genomics (a cohort, a nationality or ancestry, a disease abbreviation), or whether each of those is plainly absent from an MSK-IMPACT esophagogastric adenocarcinoma cohort.

Both treated the pooled 6-class SNV spectrum (C>T share) as an aging-signature proxy. Neither separated clock-like CpG C>T from SBS17-type T>G, and neither checked whether clock-like counts rise with age.
unused_evidence: AGE_AT_SAMPLING in data_clinical_sample.txt. An aging signature should scale with age, and team A lists this check as not done.
COHORT (Curative/Palliative) and the patient-level fields. These are the study's own groupings and the only candidate 'subgroups' that 'JP' could conceivably map to.
MSI_SCORE and TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS. These flag hypermutated or MSI samples whose signatures would distort a pooled spectrum.
unresolved_weak_points: Both teams named the identity of 'JP' as their weakest point and only reported it. Neither resolved it beyond a grep, and their confidences are about 0.55-0.6.
Team B noted that C>T dominates (54.4%) and would lean True if 'JP' meant this cohort. It did not test whether that C>T is CpG/clock-like or driven by hotspots.
second_readings: 'JP' could name a population or cohort, for example Japanese patients. A population the tables do not record would make the hypothesis come from another publication, which supports Not verifiable. It could also be a garbled abbreviation for this study's own cohort, which would call for True or False.
'Dominant' could mean the largest signature share in the pooled cohort, or the top signature in most individual tumours.
challenge.verdict: Moderate trust. No table encodes 'JP', and the cohort is an EAC panel study where SBS17 rather than aging is usually the hallmark, so Not verifiable under the benchmark convention is plausible. The label hinges entirely on what 'JP' means, and neither team resolved that.

questions.question: QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Beyond grepping for 'JP', list which kinds of entity 'JP' could plausibly abbreviate (a population or nationality, a disease or histology, a cohort). For each, check whether any column (COHORT, SEX, CANCER_TYPE_DETAILED, ONCOTREE_CODE, SAMPLE_TYPE_DETAIL, ID prefixes) could encode it. Does the result change your Not verifiable decision?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: You list the age correlation of clock-like counts as not done. Correlate the per-sample CpG C>T count (panel-normalised) with AGE_AT_SAMPLING. Does the result change how much weight your secondary spectrum check deserves?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Split your 54.4% C>T into CpG and non-CpG and remove hotspot and recurrent positions, as team A did. Also report the T>G fraction. Does the clock-like share stay dominant, and does that change the confidence or reasoning behind your label?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Check whether 'JP' could map to the study's own patient groupings (COHORT Curative/Palliative, Pre-Tx vs Post-Tx samples) or to a population not recorded in the tables. If it maps to an unrecorded population or disease, does that confirm Not verifiable under the benchmark convention, and if it maps to a study group, would you switch to True or False?
In cancer genomics and mutational-signature literature, what does the abbreviation 'JP' most commonly denote (for example, a population such as Japanese patients, or a tumour type)?
questions.why: The label depends on whether 'JP' names an entity covered by the study. Neither team established its meaning.

questions.question: Can COSMIC SBS1/SBS5 aging signatures be reliably estimated from targeted gene-panel (~400-500 gene) somatic mutation calls without trinucleotide context, and what minimum mutation counts are recommended?
questions.why: This decides whether the spectrum evidence can bear any weight if the hypothesis turns out to concern this cohort.

findings.question: In cancer genomics and mutational-signature literature, what does the abbreviation 'JP' most commonly denote (for example, a population such as Japanese patients, or a tumour type)?
findings.answer: The web did not settle this: the research gateway returned HTTP 403 on both search and contents, so no pages were read. From prior knowledge, 'JP' most commonly appears as the ISO country code for Japan in ICGC project names (e.g. LIRI-JP), which denotes Japanese cohorts. It is not a standard tumour-type abbreviation; juvenile polyposis is usually 'JPS'. Nothing links 'JP' to an MSK-IMPACT esophagogastric adenocarcinoma cohort. So if no column in the tables maps to JP, the hypothesis probably concerns a cohort these tables do not cover, which points to Not verifiable under the benchmark convention.

findings.question: Can COSMIC SBS1/SBS5 aging signatures be reliably estimated from targeted gene-panel (~400-500 gene) somatic mutation calls without trinucleotide context, and what minimum mutation counts are recommended?
findings.answer: The web did not settle this: the gateway returned HTTP 403 and no pages were read. From prior knowledge, the answer is no. These signatures cannot be estimated per sample from panels of about 1 Mb, where most samples have fewer than 10 SNVs. Signature fitting needs the 96-channel trinucleotide context, though it can be rebuilt from a reference genome. Panel-specific tools such as SigMA (Gulhan et al. 2019) target strong signatures like SBS3 or MMR. Commonly cited rules of thumb are at least about 50-100 SNVs per sample for refitting, and far more for de novo extraction. Flat SBS5/SBS40 tend to be overcalled when counts are low. Pooled cohort spectra give only coarse evidence, so the spectrum data can bear little weight.
